Hammad Foundation · logo competition · due before 20 Nov 2026

undefined ways to say 11 Years

The shortlist for the anniversary mark that sits beside the existing logo, picked from nine first sketches. Every direction keeps the emblem, the gold numerals and the “Years” ribbon so it reads as the sequel to the 10 Years mark.

  • Emblem unchanged
  • Gold and green palette
  • “Years” ribbon
  • Legible at 70 px

The problem. In the 10 Years mark the round emblem stands in for the 0. “11” has no zero, and putting the emblem after “11” reads as “110”. Every direction below gives the emblem a new job.

Direction E1

Twin Trees · Canopy

The two 1s become tree trunks. Their roots link at the base, and the emblem is the canopy they hold up together.

Story
Planted together, growing together: hath mai hath in the roots, and the Green Initiatives and plantation drives in the trees.
How it reads
A single tree shape at a glance. The two trunks and their side branches still carry the “11” underneath the crown.
Watch out
The emblem covers the tops of the 1s, so “11” is the second read. Test it at 32 px before going further.

concepts/svg/E1-tree-canopy.svg

Direction F

Two Hands

Each 1 becomes a hand and forearm. The two hands cup the emblem from below and lift it up like a globe.

Story
The foundation held up by its people: hath mai hath do, Hammad ka sath do. The emblem’s four quadrants become the world they carry.
How it reads
Reads as care and support first. The two upright forearms carry the “11”, and the thumbs echo the flag of each 1.
Watch out
“11” is the subtlest of all the directions. It may need “11” on the ribbon (as in D) to be read as a number.

concepts/svg/F-two-hands.svg

Direction G2

Line Grove · Circle

The same continuous line, traced as a circle that echoes the emblem’s round shape before turning inward as the “11”.

Story
Everything flows out from the foundation and grows back toward it, and the circle ties the mark to the emblem and to the 10 Years silhouette.
How it reads
Feels like a sibling of the emblem, as if the emblem’s ring has unwound into two growing stems.
Watch out
A big ring around a small emblem can look like a second, larger emblem, so the line weight needs care.

concepts/svg/G2-line-grove-circle.svg

Direction H1

Doorway · Skyline

Two door-shaped 1s are cut into a deep-green tile, like the master logo’s square. Through them you see the sky and a city, with light spilling out onto two small figures.

Story
Eleven years open the door to what comes next: the way through to “Transforming Pakistan by 2050”, walked by real people.
How it reads
The openings are the numerals, so “11” reads as light against the dark wall. No font is needed.
Watch out
The skyline and figures disappear below about 40 px, so H2 is the version for favicons and small use.

concepts/svg/H1-doorway-skyline.svg

Direction H2

Doorway · Light

The same two doorways, with nothing but gold light coming through. The bold, minimal version.

Story
As H1, cut down to the essentials: dark wall, two bright 1s and the emblem on top.
How it reads
The strongest “11” at small sizes, since two solid gold shapes on dark green survive even at 16 px.
Watch out
With the scene removed it relies on the light alone, so the gold gradient must stay warm and clean when printed.

concepts/svg/H2-doorway-light.svg

Direction H3

Doorway · ۱۱ Calligraphic

The openings take the shape of the Urdu numeral ۱, a pen stroke that is broad at the top and tapers to the floor. The ribbon reads سال (years) in Nastaliq.

Story
One mark that reads “11” in English and “۱۱” in Urdu. It roots the anniversary in the language of the people the foundation serves, and echoes the gold Urdu calligraphy on its website.
How it reads
Two bright vertical strokes read as 11 to everyone. Urdu readers also see the calligraphic ۱۱ and the word سال.
Watch out
The tapered strokes are thinner at the floor, so the light spill is narrower. Nastaliq on the ribbon needs a proper Urdu font when finalised.

concepts/svg/H3-doorway-urdu.svg

Direction H4

Doorway · Mehrab

Two tall pointed Mughal arches, like the doorways of mosques and the Mazar-e-Quaid, cut into the green tile, with سال on the ribbon.

Story
Pakistani heritage architecture as the way forward: two gateways that read as ۱۱ and 11.
How it reads
Instantly local and dignified. The arches still read as two 1s because they are tall, narrow and side by side.
Watch out
Arches lean toward a religious or monument feel. Check that it suits a civic foundation rather than reading as a mosque mark.

concepts/svg/H4-doorway-mehrab.svg

Execution on different backgrounds

Where it will actually live

The doorway tile (H) carries its own green, so it holds up everywhere except deep green, where it needs a keyline. G2’s green ring disappears on greens and photos, and every gold element struggles on hi-vis lime, so vests need a one-colour version.
